y'=\frac{x - 1}{y},\quad y(1)=-2.
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-4(x + 4){y}^{2} & =4(x + 4) \\ 2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =4(x + 4){y}^{2}+4(x + 4) \\ 2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =4(x + 4)({y}^{2}+1) \\ \frac{2y}{{y}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}y & =4(x + 4)\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{2y}{{y}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}y & =\int 4(x + 4)\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}+1) & =2{(x + 4)}^{2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Exponentiating both sides, we find the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}+1)} & ={e}^{2{(x + 4)}^{2}+C} \\ {y}^{2}+1 & =C{e}^{2{(x + 4)}^{2}} \\ y & =\sqrt{C{e}^{2{(x + 4)}^{2}}-1}\end{aligned}
$$

where we used that $y>0.$

We now apply the initial condition $y(-4)=1$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(-4) & =1 \\ \sqrt{C{e}^{2(0)^{2}}-1} & =1 \\ \sqrt{C-1} & =1 \\ C-1 & =1 \\ C & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the particular solution is

$$
y(x)=\sqrt{2{e}^{2{(x + 4)}^{2}}-1}.
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{e}^{-y} & =6{(x + 4)}^{2}{e}^{-y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =6{(x + 4)}^{2}{e}^{-y}-{e}^{-y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =(6{(x + 4)}^{2}-1){e}^{-y} \\ {e}^{y}\,\text{d}y & =(6{(x + 4)}^{2}-1)\,\text{d}x \\ \int {e}^{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int (6{(x + 4)}^{2}-1)\,\text{d}x \\ {e}^{y} & =2{(x + 4)}^{3}-(x + 4)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the natural logarithm to both sides, we find the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{y}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2{(x + 4)}^{3}-(x + 4)+C) \\ y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2{(x + 4)}^{3}-(x + 4)+C)\end{aligned}
$$

We now apply the initial condition $y(-3)=0$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(-3) & =0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(2\cdot {1}^{3}-1+C) & =0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(1+C) & =0 \\ C & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the particular solution is

$$
y(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2{(x + 4)}^{3}-(x + 4)).
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={e}^{4(x - 1)-y}$ that satisfies $y(1)=5.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{4(x - 1)-y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{4(x - 1)}\cdot {e}^{-y} \\ {e}^{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{4(x - 1)} \\ \int {e}^{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{4(x - 1)}\,\text{d}x \\ \int {e}^{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int {e}^{4(x - 1)}\,\text{d}x \\ {e}^{y} & =\frac{{e}^{4(x - 1)}}{4}+C\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the natural logarithm to both sides, we find the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{y}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{{e}^{4(x - 1)}}{4}+C) \\ y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{{e}^{4(x - 1)}}{4}+C)\end{aligned}
$$

We now apply the condition $y(1)=5$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & =5 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{{e}^{4\cdot 0}}{4}+C) & =5 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{4}+C) & =5 \\ \frac{1}{4}+C & ={e}^{5} \\ C & =\frac{4{e}^{5}-1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the particular solution of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={e}^{4(x - 1)-y}$ that satisfies the condition $y(1)=5$ is

$$
y=\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{{e}^{4(x - 1)}+4{e}^{5}-1}{4}\right).
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $(\frac{1}{(x - 1)y}+\frac{1}{y})\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=1$ that satisfies $y(2)=e.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(\frac{1}{(x - 1)y}+\frac{1}{y})\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \frac{1}{y}\left(\frac{1+(x - 1)}{(x - 1)}\right)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \frac{1}{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{(x - 1)}{(x - 1)+1} \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{(x - 1)}{(x - 1)+1}\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int (1-\frac{1}{(x - 1)+1})\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & =(x - 1)-\operatorname{ln}⁡|(x - 1)+1|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the exponential function to both sides, we find the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|} & ={e}^{(x - 1)-\operatorname{ln}⁡|(x - 1)+1|+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{(x - 1)-\operatorname{ln}⁡|(x - 1)+1|+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{(x - 1)}\cdot {e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡|(x - 1)+1|}\cdot {e}^{C} \\ y & =\frac{K{e}^{(x - 1)}}{(x - 1)+1},\end{aligned}
$$

where $K=\pm {e}^{C}$ is an arbitrary constant. 

We now apply the initial condition $y(2)=e$ to find $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(2) & =e \\ \frac{K{e}^{1}}{1+1} & =e \\ K & =2\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the particular solution of $(\frac{1}{(x - 1)y}+\frac{1}{y})\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=1$ that satisfies the condition $y(2)=e$ is

$$
y=\frac{2{e}^{(x - 1)}}{(x - 1)+1}\,.
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the specific solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={e}^{(x - 1)+y}$ given that  $\,y(1)=-\operatorname{ln}⁡2.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{(x - 1)+y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{(x - 1)}{e}^{y} \\ {e}^{-y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{(x - 1)} \\ \int {e}^{-y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{(x - 1)}\,\text{d}x \\ \int {e}^{-y}\,\text{d}y & =\int {e}^{(x - 1)}\,\text{d}x \\ -{e}^{-y} & ={e}^{(x - 1)}+{C}_{1} \\ {e}^{-y} & =-{e}^{(x - 1)}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the natural logarithm to both sides, we find the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-y}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(-{e}^{(x - 1)}+C) \\ -y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(C-{e}^{(x - 1)}) \\ y & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡(C-{e}^{(x - 1)}).\end{aligned}
$$

We now apply the condition $y(1)=-\operatorname{ln}⁡2$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\ -\operatorname{ln}⁡(C-{e}^{0}) & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(C-1) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\ C-1 & =2 \\ C & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the particular solution of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={e}^{(x - 1)+y}$ that satisfies the condition $y(1)=-\operatorname{ln}⁡2$ is

$$
y=-\operatorname{ln}⁡(3-{e}^{(x - 1)}).
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={e}^{(x - 1)-2y}$ that satisfies $y(1)=0.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{(x - 1)-2y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{(x - 1)}\cdot {e}^{-2y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{e}^{(x - 1)}}{{e}^{2y}} \\ {e}^{2y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{(x - 1)} \\ \int {e}^{2y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{(x - 1)}\,\text{d}x \\ \int {e}^{2y}\,\text{d}y & =\int {e}^{(x - 1)}\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2y} & ={e}^{(x - 1)}+{C}_{1} \\ {e}^{2y} & =2{e}^{(x - 1)}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=2{C}_{1}$ is an arbitrary constant.

Applying the natural logarithm to both sides, we find the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{2y}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2{e}^{(x - 1)}+C) \\ y & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2{e}^{(x - 1)}+C).\end{aligned}
$$

We now apply the condition $y(1)=0$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & =0 \\ \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2{e}^{0}+C) & =0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(2+C) & =0 \\ 2+C & =1 \\ C & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the particular solution of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={e}^{(x - 1)-2y}$ that satisfies the condition $y(1)=0$ is

$$
y=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2{e}^{(x - 1)}-1).
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation ${e}^{(x - 1)}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-2(x - 1){e}^{(x - 1)}=3$ that satisfies $y(1)=-3.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{(x - 1)}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-2(x - 1){e}^{(x - 1)} & =3 \\ {e}^{(x - 1)}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3+2(x - 1){e}^{(x - 1)} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3{e}^{-(x - 1)}+2(x - 1) \\ \int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (3{e}^{-(x - 1)}+2(x - 1))\,\text{d}x \\ \int \,\text{d}y & =\int 3{e}^{-(x - 1)}\,\text{d}x+\int 2(x - 1)\,\text{d}x \\ y & =-3{e}^{-(x - 1)}+{(x - 1)}^{2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We now apply the initial condition $y(1)=-3$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & =-3 \\ -3{e}^{-0}+{0}^{2}+C & =-3 \\ C-3 & =-3 \\ C & =0\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the particular solution of ${e}^{(x - 1)}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-2(x - 1){e}^{(x - 1)}=3$ that satisfies the condition $y(1)=-3$ is

$$
y={(x - 1)}^{2}-3{e}^{-(x - 1)}.
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{e}^{-y}=4{(x - 1)}^{3}{e}^{-y}$ that satisfies $y(2)=0.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{e}^{-y} & =4{(x - 1)}^{3}{e}^{-y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =4{(x - 1)}^{3}{e}^{-y}-{e}^{-y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =(4{(x - 1)}^{3}-1){e}^{-y} \\ {e}^{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =4{(x - 1)}^{3}-1 \\ \int {e}^{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (4{(x - 1)}^{3}-1)\,\text{d}x \\ \int {e}^{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int (4{(x - 1)}^{3}-1)\,\text{d}x \\ {e}^{y} & ={(x - 1)}^{4}-(x - 1)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the natural logarithm to both sides, we find the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{y}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({(x - 1)}^{4}-(x - 1)+C) \\ y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({(x - 1)}^{4}-(x - 1)+C)\end{aligned}
$$

We now apply the initial condition $y(2)=0$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(2) & =0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({1}^{4}-1+C) & =0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡C & =0 \\ C & =1\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the particular solution of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{e}^{-y}=4{(x - 1)}^{3}{e}^{-y}$ that satisfies the condition $y(2)=0$ is

$$
y=\operatorname{ln}⁡({(x - 1)}^{4}-(x - 1)+1).
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $3{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-2(x - 1){y}^{3}=4(x - 1)$ that satisfies $y(1)=1.$  Assume that $y>0.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-2(x - 1){y}^{3} & =4(x - 1) \\ 3{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2(x - 1)(2+{y}^{3}) \\ \frac{3{y}^{2}}{2+{y}^{3}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2(x - 1) \\ \int \frac{3{y}^{2}}{2+{y}^{3}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int 2(x - 1)\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{3{y}^{2}}{2+{y}^{3}}\,\text{d}y & ={(x - 1)}^{2}+{C}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate the integral on the left-hand side of this equality, we use a substitution

$$
u=2+{y}^{3}\,⟹\,\text{d}u=3{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Then  we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3{y}^{2}}{2+{y}^{3}}\text{d}y & =\int \frac{1}{2+{y}^{3}}(3{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y) \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+{C}_{2} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+{y}^{3})+{C}_{2},\end{aligned}
$$

where we used that $y>0.$

Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+{y}^{3})+{C}_{2} & ={(x - 1)}^{2}+{C}_{1} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(2+{y}^{3}) & ={(x - 1)}^{2}+{C}_{1}-{C}_{2} \\ {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+{y}^{3})} & ={e}^{{(x - 1)}^{2}+{C}_{1}-{C}_{2}} \\ 2+{y}^{3} & =K{e}^{{(x - 1)}^{2}} \\ {y}^{3} & =K{e}^{{(x - 1)}^{2}}-2,\end{aligned}
$$

where $K={e}^{{C}_{1}-{C}_{2}}$ is an arbitrary constant. 

We now apply the initial condition $y(1)=1$ to find $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{1}^{3} & =K{e}^{{0}^{2}}-2 \\ 1 & =K-2 \\ K & =3\,.\end{aligned}
$$

So we get the particular solution in implicit form:

$$
{y}^{3}=3{e}^{{(x - 1)}^{2}}-2.
$$

We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{4{y}^{2}}{{(x - 1)}^{2}}+{y}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={y}^{2}(\frac{4}{{(x - 1)}^{2}}+1) \\ \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y & =(4{(x - 1)}^{-2}+1)\,\text{d}x \\ \int {y}^{-2}\,\text{d}y & =\int (4{(x - 1)}^{-2}+1)\,\text{d}x \\ -{y}^{-1} & =-4{(x - 1)}^{-1}+(x - 1)+C \\ -\frac{1}{y} & =-\frac{4}{(x - 1)}+(x - 1)+C\end{aligned}
$$

Solving for $y$, we find the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{y} & =\frac{4}{(x - 1)}-(x - 1)-C \\ \frac{1}{y} & =\frac{4-{(x - 1)}^{2}-C(x - 1)}{(x - 1)} \\ y & =\frac{(x - 1)}{4-{(x - 1)}^{2}-C(x - 1)}\end{aligned}
$$

We now apply the initial condition $y(3)=-1$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(3) & =-1 \\ \frac{2}{4-{2}^{2}-C(2)} & =-1 \\ \frac{2}{-2C} & =-1 \\ -\frac{1}{C} & =-1 \\ C & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the particular solution is

$$
y(x)=\frac{(x - 1)}{4-(x - 1)-{(x - 1)}^{2}}.
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2y(x - 1)+y{(x - 1)}^{2}$ that satisfies $y(2)=1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2y(x - 1)+y{(x - 1)}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =y(x^{2} + 2 x + 1) \\ \frac{1}{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2(x - 1)+{(x - 1)}^{2} \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (2(x - 1)+{(x - 1)}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =2\int (x - 1)\,\text{d}x+\int {(x - 1)}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & ={(x - 1)}^{2}+\frac{{(x - 1)}^{3}}{3}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the exponential function to both sides, we find the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|} & ={e}^{{(x - 1)}^{2}+{(x - 1)}^{3}/3+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{{(x - 1)}^{2}+{(x - 1)}^{3}/3+C} \\ y & =\pm {e}^{{(x - 1)}^{2}+{(x - 1)}^{3}/3+C} \\ y & =K{e}^{{(x - 1)}^{2}+{(x - 1)}^{3}/3},\end{aligned}
$$

where $K=\pm {e}^{C}$ is an arbitrary constant. 

We now apply the initial condition $y(2)=1$ to find $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(2) & =1 \\ K{e}^{{1}^{2}+{1}^{3}/3} & =1 \\ K{e}^{4/3} & =1 \\ K & ={e}^{-4/3}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the particular solution of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2y(x - 1)+y{(x - 1)}^{2}$ that satisfies the condition $y(2)=1$ is

$$
y={e}^{-4/3}\cdot {e}^{{(x - 1)}^{2}+{(x - 1)}^{3}/3}={e}^{({(x - 1)}^{3}+3{(x - 1)}^{2}-4)/3}\,.
$$
